source.title_on_document: Who Is the Best Helper for University Students' Mathematical Creativity? A Quasi-Experimental Study of Human–ChatGPT, Human–Google, and Human–Human Co-Creation

supplement.where: Wiley online Supporting Information section ('Appendix. Supporting document.', p. 16)
supplement.holds: Scoring reference tables for the MCT adapted from Lee and Seo (p. 6, Section 5) and Appendix Tables A1 and A3 with exploratory correlations among self-evaluation, perceived usefulness, self-efficacy, and performance (pp. 10-12). The main creativity statistics (Table 3, Section 6.1) are in the main text.

paper_design_summary: 230 Chinese university student volunteers were assigned by lottery to solve four open-ended mathematical creativity tasks with ChatGPT (60), with Google Search only (60), or in human-human dyads (110 people, 55 dyads) in which one student led and the other only supported. All participants first solved a baseline number-pyramid task alone. Solutions were scored by two scorers for flexibility (number of correct answer categories), fluency (number of correct answers), and originality (rarity of answer categories); self-evaluations, interest, difficulty, effort, partner usefulness, and self-efficacy were self-reported.

studies.label: Mathematical creativity tasks with ChatGPT vs Google Search vs human peer

assignment.what_was_assigned: Co-creation partner condition: human–ChatGPT, human–Google, or human–human (dyad). Pairs in the human–human condition were also randomly formed, with one person (A) in a leadership role.
assignment.quote: Each student was randomly assigned to one of the three experimental conditions (human–ChatGPT group, human–Google group, or human–human group) using a lottery system.
assignment.locator: p. 3, Section 3.1 Procedure (title and abstract, p. 1, call the design a quasi-experiment)

arms.name: Human–ChatGPT
arms.description: Student works alone on a personal computer with ChatGPT open in one browser tab; told how to prompt and refine; no one used other web search.

arms.name: Human–Google
arms.description: Student works alone with Google Search only; other AI tools and search engines blocked.

arms.name: Human–human
arms.description: Randomly formed student pairs; person A leads and does the work, person B supports passively without completing any work independently.

participants.exclusions: None: 'Each participant completed all the required tasks, and none were excluded' (p. 3). The human–human arm's 110 people form 55 dyads and enter the creativity analyses as 55 units: the ANOVAs have F(2, 172), i.e., 175 units (60 + 60 + 55), and the human–human t-tests have df 54. Whether the 55 units are dyad outputs or person A's output is not stated.
participants.who: Volunteer Chinese university students from all majors, rewarded with a few course credits; mean age about 19; no specific mathematics background.
participants.quote: A total of 230 Chinese university students participated in this study. ... the human–ChatGPT group contained 60 participants, the human–Google group contained 60 participants, and the human–human group contained 110 participants (55 dyads).

ai_tool.how_used: Free use of ChatGPT in a single browser tab while solving the MCT; participants were told ChatGPT responds to prompts, that more background gives more accurate responses, that they could ask for modifications, and that they could upload images or documents. Participants were encouraged to draw inspiration from their partner.

task.description: Mathematical creativity tasks (MCT) adapted from Lee and Seo: four open-ended geometry/statistics tasks asking for as many solutions as possible (2 cm² figures on a 4 x 4 grid; methods to measure dispersion of marbles; properties of water in a tilted prism; shapes sharing features with shape A). Scored for flexibility, fluency, and originality like a divergent-thinking test. Baseline: number-pyramid task solved alone before treatment.
task.duration: Whole study 80 min (SD 7) in human–ChatGPT, 70 min (SD 5) in human–Google, 68 min (SD 7.8) in human–human (p. 3)

outcomes.name: MCT flexibility
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of correct answer categories in each task, summed over the four tasks; answers coded correct/wrong and categorized by two scorers (Cohen's kappa 0.85 on 18 pre-study samples, above 0.91 on the rest, discrepancies resolved to 100% agreement). Z-standardized for the mixed ANOVA with baseline; ANCOVA with prior math competence as robustness (p. 8).

contrasts.reported: MCT (flexibility): Human–ChatGPT M = 15.03 (SD 3.78, N = 60) vs Human–Google M = 12.83 (SD 3.29, N = 60); three-group F(2, 172) = 9.71, η2p = 0.10, p < 0.001 (Bonferroni). Mixed ANOVA condition x time interaction F(2, 172) = 6.08, η2p = 0.07, p < 0.01. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
MCT (flexibility): Human–ChatGPT M = 15.03 (SD 3.78, N = 60) vs Human–human M = 12.38 (SD 3.35, 55 dyads); three-group F(2, 172) = 9.71, η2p = 0.10, p < 0.001. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
Human–ChatGPT flexibility increased, t(59) = 2.48, p < 0.050, d = 0.44; human–human t(54) = 2.24, p < 0.050, d = 0.36; human–Google t(59) = 0.71, p = 0.483, d = 0.11 (Bonferroni post hoc).

outcomes.name: MCT fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of correct answers in each category (maximum five points per category), summed over the four tasks; same scorers and z-standardization as flexibility; ANCOVA with prior math competence as robustness.

contrasts.reported: MCT (fluency): Human–ChatGPT M = 27.85 (SD 7.56, N = 60) vs Human–Google M = 23.78 (SD 6.50, N = 60); three-group F(2, 172) = 7.91, η2p = 0.08, p = 0.001 (Bonferroni). Mixed ANOVA interaction F(2, 172) = 4.68, η2p = 0.05, p < 0.05. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
MCT (fluency): Human–ChatGPT M = 27.85 (SD 7.56, N = 60) vs Human–human M = 23.42 (SD 5.93, 55 dyads); three-group F(2, 172) = 7.91, η2p = 0.08, p = 0.001. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
Human–ChatGPT fluency increased, t(59) = 2.14, p < 0.050, d = 0.39; human–Google t(59) = 0.80, p = 0.426, d = 0.13; human–human t(54) = 1.90, p = 0.064, d = 0.31.

outcomes.name: MCT originality
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Rarity of answer categories: share of each answer category among all responses; categories with share in (0, 1%), (1%, 2%), (2%, 3%) score 3, 2, 1; summed over the four tasks. Coded by the two scorers. Z-standardized for the mixed ANOVA (Figure 2 plots z-scores); ANCOVA with prior math competence as robustness.

contrasts.reported: MCT (originality): Human–ChatGPT M = 5.47 (SD 2.83, N = 60) vs Human–Google M = 3.88 (SD 2.32, N = 60); three-group F(2, 172) = 18.31, η2p = 0.18, p < 0.001 (Bonferroni). Mixed ANOVA interaction F(2, 172) = 8.19, η2p = 0.09, p < 0.001. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 7, Table 3 row 4; pp. 7-8, Section 6.1; p. 8, Figure 2

contrasts.reported: MCT (originality): Human–ChatGPT M = 5.47 (SD 2.83, N = 60) vs Human–human M = 7.00 (SD 3.10, 55 dyads); three-group F(2, 172) = 18.31, η2p = 0.18, p < 0.001. Text: 'the human–human group achieved greater originality than the other groups'. No pairwise between-arm test printed.
Human–ChatGPT originality did not change, t(59) = 0.12, p = 0.906, d = 0.02; human–Google decreased, t(59) = 3.14, p < 0.010, d = 0.48; human–human increased, t(54) = 2.73, p < 0.010, d = 0.45.

eligibility.reason: Students were assigned by lottery to ChatGPT, Google Search, or a human peer (p. 3), so ChatGPT is compared with other aids (ai_vs_active); the paper nonetheless calls itself a quasi-experiment in the title and abstract. 230 people analyzed with none excluded (120 in the ChatGPT vs Google contrast alone; the human-human arm enters as 55 dyad units). Flexibility, fluency, and originality are scored on the solutions by two coders (p. 6).

one_line_finding: With ChatGPT, students scored higher on flexibility (15.03 vs 12.83 Google, 12.38 peer dyads) and fluency (27.85 vs 23.78, 23.42) but lower on originality than peer dyads (5.47 vs 7.00; Google 3.88); three-group F tests p <= 0.001 (p. 7, Table 3).
open_questions: The title and abstract call the study a quasi-experiment while Section 3.1 (p. 3) describes individual random assignment by lottery; the reason for the quasi label is not given.
Group sizes (60, 60, 110) are unequal for a lottery with equal chances; the paper does not explain how the lottery produced them.
In the human-human arm only 55 units enter the analyses (df 54; F(2, 172)); the paper does not say whether the scored output is the dyad's joint output or person A's.

No pairwise between-arm tests are printed for the creativity outcomes; Table 3 gives three-group F tests on (apparently raw) MCT scores, and the post hoc tests in Section 6.1 are within-group pre-post changes in z-scores across different tasks (baseline vs MCT).
The retrieval notes mention a separate AJET paper by overlapping authors (Liu, Li, Zuo, Lu, Feng) on ChatGPT and mathematical creativity; this PDF does not cite it or state any shared sample.
notes: Self-reported outcomes (self-evaluation of flexibility/fluency/originality, bias index, interest, difficulty, effort, partner usefulness, contributions, self-efficacy) are not listed as outcomes because they are not scored on the output (Table 3 rows 5-18). The baseline creativity task was solved alone before treatment (Table 3 row 1: 15.53 vs 15.15 vs 15.91, F = 0.21, p = 0.808), so it is a pre-treatment measure, not an after_ai outcome. ANCOVA with prior math competence (p. 8) is a robustness variant. The ChatGPT arm also took longer overall (80 vs 70 vs 68 min).
